name: BLS Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW)
gap: employment/wage growth as a demand-side predictor, no current equivalent in the screener (BLS named explicitly in this run's instructions)
measures: Employment counts and average weekly wages by industry (NAICS), covering >95% of U.S. jobs reported by employers, at county/MSA/state/national level.
granularity: county (and MSA/state/national roll-ups) — no tract or ZIP breakdown
update_frequency: quarterly, released ~6 months after quarter-end (e.g. Q1 2026 county data releases August 28, 2026 per BLS's posted schedule)

fits_existing_gap_in_code: No current source touches local employment or wages. The closest existing pillar is 'demographics' (census_acs.py: population, income, education, age), which is ACS income level/growth, not employment growth — QCEW would add a distinct, higher-frequency (quarterly vs ACS's 5-year rolling) jobs signal.
recommendation: Lean recommend, with a granularity caveat. QCEW is free, government, long-history and exactly in the requested source list, but it's county-level — all five NYC boroughs are each their own county, so it gives only 5 distinct values across this app's 262 NTAs today, meaning it can't differentiate neighborhoods within a borough (it would either be dropped at NTA-percentile granularity or applied flatly per-borough, both weak). Its real payoff is for CLAUDE.md's stated 'generalizing to any US neighborhood' goal: in most of the country outside NYC, county is a normal and useful granularity for a local job-growth signal, and QCEW is the standard free source for it. Worth implementing once (or as part of) the area-model/CBSA migration mentioned in backend/CLAUDE.md, rather than as a priority add to the current NYC-NTA screener.
